Two mechanisms, deliberately different in strength. STATE: every tab has a stable slice id (fleet agent id if spawned, else the sessionStorage tab id); state_push/state_pull take scope: 'agent' and write under state/agents/<id>/, a sibling of the shared tree, so two tabs hold divergent state without clobbering each other or the operator's. GRAPH: all tabs keep sharing ONE quipu store — a fleet whose agents cannot see what each other learned is not worth running — and each tab stamps the episodes it ingests with group_id agent:<id>, so facts are scoped/reviewable/retractable per agent while reads stay fleet-wide. An explicit group_id from the caller always wins. 11 new assertions in tests/test-state.js, including that withScope does not leak and that reads are never silently scoped.

extra.new_value: Fleet has no test of its own

creel-fleet.js is 1122 lines and creel-self.js 805, both well past the point where a reader can hold them. Same disease as onepagent.html — but NOT the same cure. The harness split was mechanical because it was one flat script: classic scripts share a global lexical environment, so moving a line between files changed nothing. These two are IIFEs, so splitting them means restructuring a closure and re-exposing its internals through a namespace. That is a real refactor, not a move.

BLOCKED ON creel-psr. creel-fleet.js owns Web Locks leasing, crash detection, heartbeats and the cross-tab bus, and has no test of its own. Restructuring that with nothing to catch a regression risks a bug that only appears under real parallelism and reads as flakiness when it does. Write the fleet test first, then split.

creel-self.js is the safer half and could go first: its seams (locator bridge / tool surface / UI reach) are covered by test-ui-crosstab and test-ui-browser.

extra.reason: tests/test-fleet.js: 8 assertions, real tabs in real Chromium, real Web Locks and IndexedDB, only handleSend stubbed. Covers claim exclusivity under a genuine two-worker race (and that the loser does not claim a moment later), death-releases-lease with the survivor picking it up, heartbeat-stale requeue while the lock is still held, drain, and the work log. It immediately found a real bug: tx() resolved a MISSING get to the IDBRequest instead of undefined, so every '(await getTask(id)) || {default}' skipped its fallback — the fleet work log's record was never created and fleet_digest had never returned a single entry. Fixed by unwrapping on type rather than on whether the result happened to be undefined.

creel-self.js 805 -> 301 + creel-ui-tools.js 423 + creel-world-model.js 155. creel-fleet.js 1150 -> 562 + creel-fleet-tools.js 422 + creel-fleet-dashboard.js 207 + creel-fleet-log.js 82. Largest file in app/ is now 571. Not a move like the harness split: these were IIFEs, so each group shares one documented internal namespace (CreelSelfInternal / CreelFleetInternal) rather than dumping ~40 names into the global scope. The lease state deliberately does not cross the fleet seam — currentLeaseTaskId and its lock resolver only stay in agreement if one place changes them, so the seam carries heldLease()/releaseLease() instead. Verified by the full suite plus the new creel-psr leasing test; test-ui-crosstab now loads all three self parts in page order, and the dashboard (previously uncovered) gained a mount check.

Detection came from the service worker rather than the version.json polling this bead sketched — a newer worker installing IS the deploy signal, with no extra file, no polling, and no cache-busting to get wrong. The page promotes the waiting worker and fires creel-update-ready; creel-self.js renders a dismissible role=status notice whose primary action is Save state and reload (the same path ui_reload takes). Nothing auto-reloads.

extra.reason: Measured, not guessed. renderMd re-renders the whole accumulated message (22ms at 10KB, 117ms at 40KB, 248ms at 80KB) and the throttle re-queued it 50ms after the last render STARTED, so partway through a long reply each render outlasted the gap before the next. Streaming a 167KB answer: 2545ms of main thread, 58% duty, blocks to 191ms — and worsening with length. The interval now follows measured cost (~3x, floor 50ms, cap 1s): same workload 683ms, 25% duty, and bounded by construction. tests/test-render.js drives the real throttle with a renderer of known cost so it asserts the scheduling rule rather than a flaky wall-clock number. Quipu wasm was cleared as a suspect: it boots in 430ms inside a worker.
